A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CASS and retain matching main sections, equations, and experiments. The supplied v1 ends after the references; v2 includes supplementary Sections 6–11. Text extraction and visual inspection support comparison of the complete supplied material.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation results across eight benchmark settings, component ablations, and backbone comparisons in Tables 1–4.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds encoder-scaling results, further ablations, qualitative comparisons, and application demonstrations.

M1.justification: The proposed spectral matching, low-rank eigenscaling, text-embedding adjustment, and object-prior fusion remain unchanged in Sections 3.2–3.3. Section 7 supplies previously deferred specifications of these components. The additional backbone configurations and optional postprocessing are settings for supplementary evaluations.

E1.justification: The eight segmentation benchmark settings remain unchanged. Limited additional coverage includes using segmentation masks for image inpainting and object removal in Figure 9, and cartoon-character inputs among the open-vocabulary examples in Figure 15.

E2.justification: The main quantitative baseline roster is retained. Figures 11–14 add SCLIP to qualitative comparisons that used NACLIP and ProxyCLIP in v1 Figure 6. Supplementary experiments also introduce focused comparisons with already-present baselines, including CaR for encoder scaling and NACLIP for image editing.

E3.justification: The main resizing, 224-by-224 sliding window, stride, and evaluation metrics are retained. Supplementary experiments substantially extend the controlled settings: separate scaling of the CLIP global encoder, additional DINO backbones, alternative attention features, matching strategies, and rank-selection procedures. Figure 15 additionally uses PAMR refinement, unlike the unrefined benchmark comparisons.

E4.justification: Tables 6–9 add targeted tests of VFM backbone dependence, attention-feature selection, sequential versus similar versus complementary head matching, and fixed versus adaptive rank selection. Figure 10 and Section 11 add a small-object failure analysis, while Figure 9 examines consequences of incomplete masks for downstream editing.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added experiments retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: v2 revises several Table 3 ablation values; for example, experiment 3 changes from 62.5/36.9/24.5 to 62.9/37.7/25.2 mIoU on V21/PC59/C-Stf. Tables 5–9 add substantial numerical results, alongside new qualitative and runtime findings. Headline Tables 1–2 remain unchanged, including CASS averages of 44.4 mIoU and 69.0 pAcc.

T1.justification: v2 explicitly defines the retained-energy criterion in Equation 11 and the dynamic eigenscaling function in Equation 13, which v1 described without these formulas. These are localized additions to the mathematical specification of existing components; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statements retain the same claims: training-free segmentation, improved object-level coherence through spectral distillation, object-presence-guided refinement, and strong benchmark performance. The shortened conclusion preserves their scientific meaning.

C2.justification: Section 11 adds substantive limitations absent from v1: expensive eigendecomposition, CPU matching latency, insufficient real-time speed, weaker small-object performance, and missing temporal consistency. Supplementary analyses also introduce interpretations of feature choice, matching strategy, and adaptive rank selection, substantially expanding the discussion of mechanisms and applicability.

D1.justification: v2 adds rank-selection and clustering pseudocode, the eigenscaling parameter of 1.5, cosine-distance clustering with Ward linkage, averaging over 80 prompt templates, and dataset-specific alpha/gamma values in Table 11. It also identifies CPU matching and RTX A6000 hardware. These disclosures materially improve reproducibility without establishing changes to the original experiments.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations including SAM, LaMa, and recent attention-grounding studies, and supplies the correct PnP-OVSS reference for the existing baseline row. Section 8.2.1 further contrasts CASS distillation with LaVG graph partitioning. The central research positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: Previously brief, deferred method descriptions receive substantial step-by-step explanation in a newly organized supplement, with separate implementation, applications, and discussion sections. The main narrative remains largely intact, with localized shortening in Section 4.2 and the conclusion, plus author contact information and acknowledgements.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5–11, Figures 9–15, and two algorithm displays, substantially expanding the presentation of procedures, comparisons, applications, and failures. Existing illustrations are also revised, including the input example in Figure 2 and the attention visualization in Figure 3; the main pages reflow.

improvement.justification: The supplement substantially improves methodological transparency by supplying important specifications missing from v1, and adds targeted validation and explicit computational and small-object limitations. These gains strengthen the paper despite unchanged headline scores. Some new prose overstates the evidence: Section 8.1.2 claims universal superiority over CaR, although Table 5 reports 91.4 for CaR versus 89.3 for CASS on V20 with the L/14 global encoder. This limited inconsistency does not outweigh the documentation and evaluation gains.
